passages.happening:
The long talk at the supper table is over. Now Jesus turns from his friends to his Father, and he prays aloud where they can hear him. He lifted up his eyes to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come. Glorify Your Son, that Your Son may glorify You” (verse 1).

The prayer moves outward in three circles. First Jesus prays about himself (verses 1-5). Then he prays for the friends in the room (verses 6-19). Then he prays for everyone who will believe through them, down to the present day (verses 20-26).

In this first part he says that the Father has given him authority over all people, so that he may give eternal life to those the Father has given him (verse 2). Then he says what eternal life is: “Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent” (verse 3). He has finished the work the Father gave him (verse 4). And he asks to be given back the glory he had with the Father “before the world existed” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
All through John's book the reader has been waiting for ‘the hour’. At the wedding in Cana Jesus said, “My hour has not yet come” (2:4). Twice his enemies could not arrest him, because his hour had not yet come (7:30, 8:20). Then, when some Greeks asked to see him, he said, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (12:23). Now he says it to his Father. The hour is his death.

That is what makes the word ‘glorify’ so startling. Glory means God's greatness made visible, the weight and shining of who he is. Most people would look for glory in a crown or a victory. Jesus looks for it on a cross. In John, the cross is not a defeat that Easter later repairs. It is the place where the Father's love and the Son's obedience are seen most clearly.

To lift up the eyes to heaven was a natural way to pray. A psalm says, “I lift up my eyes to You, the One enthroned in heaven” (Psalm 123:1). Jesus did the same at the tomb of Lazarus (11:41).

Verse 3 is the nearest thing in the Bible to a definition of eternal life. It is not first about how long life lasts. It is about whom you know. In the Bible, to ‘know’ God is not to know facts about him. It is to know him the way people in a covenant, a binding promise of love, know each other: to trust him, belong to him, and live with him.

Since the 1500s Christians have often called this chapter ‘the high priestly prayer’. The Lutheran teacher David Chytraeus (1530 to 1600) is usually credited with the name, though readers saw a priest praying here long before him. A high priest stood before God on behalf of the people. Some scholars think the title says more than the chapter does. But it fits what Jesus does next: he carries his friends, by name, into his Father's presence.
passages.ot:
Israel confessed every day, “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus keeps that faith when he calls the Father ‘the only true God’. And the prophet Jeremiah promised a new covenant in which no one would need to teach his neighbor, ‘Know the LORD,’ “because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jeremiah 31:34). Jesus says that this knowing is what eternal life is.

Isaiah heard God say, “I will not yield My glory to another” (Isaiah 42:8). That is what makes verse 5 so bold. Jesus asks for the glory he shared with the Father before anything was made. John opened his book with the same claim: the Word was with God in the beginning (1:1). Proverbs pictures God's Wisdom at his side at creation, “His delight day by day” (Proverbs 8:30). Jesus speaks as one who was there.
passages.hard:
If eternal life is to know ‘the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent’, does that mean Jesus is not God? Some readers have taken it that way, from Arius in the early 300s to Jehovah's Witnesses today. They are sincere, and they deserve a patient answer, not scorn.

Notice what Jesus asks for two verses later: the glory he had with the Father “before the world existed” (verse 5). God shares his glory with no created being (Isaiah 42:8). And John's first letter, using the same words, says of the Son, as most readers take it, “He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). ‘The only true God’ is set against the false gods of the nations, not against the Son. The note on 14:28 sets out how the creeds confess the Father and the Son as one God, and it applies here too.

Verse 2 raises another old question: who are ‘those You have given Him’? Some readers stress that God chooses his people. Others stress that anyone may come, as Jesus said, “everyone who believes in Him shall not perish” (3:16). Christians who stress God's choosing and those who stress human freedom have read these verses differently for centuries. These notes do not settle it.
passages.asks: Jesus says eternal life is knowing God. Not knowing about him, but knowing him. Ask whether your faith is mostly facts you hold, or a person you trust and talk to. And notice what Jesus prays for in the hour of his death. Not escape, but that the Father's glory would be seen in what he was about to suffer. Ask what it would mean to pray that prayer in your own hard hour.

passages.happening:
Now Jesus prays for the eleven friends around him. He has made the Father's name known to them. They belonged to the Father, the Father gave them to Jesus, “and they have kept Your word” (verse 6). They have come to believe that Jesus came from the Father (verses 7-8).

“I ask on their behalf. I do not ask on behalf of the world, but on behalf of those You have given Me; for they are Yours” (verse 9). He is leaving, but they are staying in the world. So he asks: “Holy Father, protect them by Your name, the name You gave Me, so that they may be one as We are one” (verse 11).

While he was with them, he kept them safe. “Not one of them has been lost, except the son of destruction, so that the Scripture would be fulfilled” (verse 12). He means Judas, who has already gone out into the night (13:30).
passages.hearers:
In Israel a name was more than a label. It stood for the person: his character, his authority, his presence. When Moses asked God's name, God gave it and said, “This is My name forever” (Exodus 3:15). To be kept ‘by Your name’ is to be kept by who God is, under his protection, the way a family is safe under a strong father's name.

Why does Jesus say he is not praying for the world? Not because he does not care about it. John has already said that “God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son” (3:16). And in verse 21 Jesus will pray for the disciples' unity “so that the world may believe”. Here he is praying for the few he is about to leave behind, the way a dying parent's last words are for the children in the room.

‘The son of destruction’ is a Hebrew way of speaking. To be the ‘son of’ something was to belong to it or be marked by it. Paul uses the same phrase for the ‘man of lawlessness’ who opposes God, calling him “the son of destruction” (2 Thessalonians 2:3). In the Greek of verse 12 there is a sad play on words. ‘Lost’ (apōleto) and ‘destruction’ (apōleia) come from the same root. None of them was lost, except the one whose path led to being lost.
passages.ot:
Jesus has already pointed to the Scripture he means. At the supper he quoted a psalm: ‘The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me’ (13:18). The psalm says, “Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9). After Jesus rose, Peter applied another psalm to Judas: “May another take his position” (Acts 1:20, quoting Psalm 109:8).

There is also a picture of a priest here. When Aaron, the first high priest, went into the Holy Place, he wore a breastpiece carved with the names of Israel's tribes. He bore “the names of the sons of Israel over his heart” before the LORD (Exodus 28:29). Jesus does something like it. He brings his friends before his Father one by one and asks him to keep them.
passages.hard:
If Judas was lost ‘so that the Scripture would be fulfilled’, did he have any choice? It is a fair and old question.

Christians have answered it in more than one way. Some say that God's plan included the betrayal, and Judas still chose it freely and was guilty of it. Peter said the same of the cross itself: Jesus “was delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge,” and yet by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). Others say that God knew ahead of time what Judas would freely do, and Scripture foretold it without forcing it. Many add that the psalm describes a pattern that keeps happening, a good man betrayed by a trusted friend, and Judas fitted it by his own choices.

John does not make Judas a puppet. He says Judas stole from the common purse (12:6). And he shows Jesus washing Judas's feet and handing him bread at the table (13:5, 13:26), signs of love to the very end. The Gospels tell what Judas did. These notes do not say what God did with Judas. That belongs to God.
passages.asks:
Jesus brought his friends before his Father by name, and he still does: the letter to the Hebrews says he “always lives to intercede” for those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). Ask whom you carry before God by name, and whether you believe that someone carries you.

Some readers fear that they are like Judas, that they have gone too far to come back. Peter also failed that same night, three times, and Jesus restored him by the lake (21:15-17). The thing to fear is not the size of a failure. It is never turning back.

passages.t: Not of the world; sanctify them by the truth
passages.happening:
Jesus says he is praying aloud now “so that they may have My joy fulfilled within them” (verse 13).

He has given them the Father's word, and the world has hated them, “for they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world” (verse 14). Yet he does not ask the Father to take them out of it: “I am not asking that You take them out of the world, but that You keep them from the evil one” (verse 15).

Then he prays, “Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth” (verse 17). He is sending them into the world, as the Father sent him (verse 18). “For them I sanctify Myself, so that they too may be sanctified by the truth” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
‘The world’ in John usually means human life organized without God and against him. It does not mean the earth, and it does not mean people as such. God loves the world and sent his Son to save it (3:16-17). But the world, in this sense, did not recognize him (1:10). So ‘not of the world’ is about where the disciples' life comes from, not where they live. They live in the world. Their life comes from God.

To ‘sanctify’ means to make holy, to set apart for God. In Israel, priests were set apart for God's service. Moses was told to ‘consecrate them so that they may serve Me as priests’ (Exodus 28:41), and the high priest wore a gold plate on his turban engraved HOLY TO THE LORD (Exodus 28:36). Sacrifices were set apart too, given wholly to God.

So when Jesus says, ‘For them I sanctify Myself’, his friends would hear a priest and a sacrifice in the same sentence. He is setting himself apart for his death, for their sake. And the Father had already set him apart: Jesus spoke of “the One whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world” (10:36). Now the same pattern passes to them. Set apart, and sent.

What sets them apart is ‘the truth’, and Jesus says plainly what that is: ‘Your word is truth’. The word is what Jesus gave them from the Father (verse 14). For the church it came to mean the Scriptures as well, through which that word still comes.
passages.ot:
God told Israel, “be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). He said to them, “you are a people holy to the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 7:6). Holiness never meant leaving the world. It meant belonging to God in the middle of it. When Israel was carried off to Babylon, Jeremiah told the exiles, “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). They were to stay God's people in a foreign city, and to work for its good.

A psalm says to God, “Your law is true” (Psalm 119:142). Jesus says the same of the Father's word: it is truth, and it is what makes a person holy.
passages.hard:
‘Not of the world’ has been misused in two opposite ways.

Some have used it to pull away from everyone outside the church and to look down on them. But Jesus says the opposite of pulling away: ‘I am not asking that You take them out of the world’ (verse 15), and ‘I have also sent them into the world’ (verse 18). This prayer gives no one leave to despise anyone. The people the church calls ‘the world’ are the people God loved enough to send his Son.

Others have used the world's love of them as proof of faithfulness, and fitted in so well that nothing marks them out. Jesus says his friends will be hated because they belong to him (verse 14). Not every bit of hostility is that, of course. Sometimes Christians are disliked because they are unkind. But a faith that never costs anything may have stopped being different.

Christians have always argued about where the line runs. Some have gone apart into communities of prayer. Others have served in the middle of city life, in politics, business and the arts. All of them have this prayer to answer to: in the world, not of it, kept from the evil one, and sent.
passages.asks: Jesus did not pray that his friends would escape. He prayed that they would be kept and sent. Ask where you have tried to hide from the world, and where you have melted into it. And ask what ‘set apart’ would look like in the place where you actually live and work this week, among people God loves.

passages.t: That they may all be one
passages.happening:
Now the prayer reaches past the room. “I am not asking on behalf of them alone, but also on behalf of those who will believe in Me through their message” (verse 20). Every Christian since, the reader included, is in this verse.

He prays “that all of them may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You. May they also be in Us, so that the world may believe that You sent Me” (verse 21). He has given them his glory so that they may be one (verse 22), and he prays “that they may be perfectly united, so that the world may know that You sent Me and have loved them just as You have loved Me” (verse 23).

He wants them with him, to see his glory, given in love “before the foundation of the world” (verse 24). The world has not known the Father, but Jesus has, and he will keep making the Father's name known, “so that the love You have for Me may be in them, and I in them” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Jesus' first followers were a handful of frightened men about to scatter. He prays for people they would never meet: Greeks, Romans, Africans, Asians, centuries of them. It is the prayer of someone who knows the message will not die with him.

Notice what kind of unity he asks for: ‘as We are one’. The pattern is the Father and the Son, a oneness of love and life, each in the other. That is more than agreement and more than an organization. And notice why: ‘so that the world may believe’. Christians' love for one another is meant to be visible, a sign that points to God.

Christians agree that this prayer matters. They disagree about what its answer looks like, and each view is held by careful, faithful people.

The Catholic Church teaches that the one church of Christ ‘subsists in’ the Catholic Church (the Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium 8), while real gifts of truth and grace are found among other Christians. In its 1964 decree on ecumenism, Unitatis Redintegratio, the Council said that division among Christians openly contradicts the will of Christ, is a scandal to the world, and harms the preaching of the gospel, and it committed the church to seek full visible unity.

Orthodox Christians teach that unity is not a goal still to be reached but a mark the church already has. It is kept in sharing one faith and one Eucharist, the Lord's Supper. For that reason they do not share communion where the faith is not shared.

Many Protestants teach that all who truly belong to Christ are already one in him, across their churches, and that unity in the truth of the gospel matters more than one organization. The Lausanne Covenant of 1974, signed by evangelicals from many nations, still affirmed ‘that the Church's visible unity in truth is God's purpose’.

In the twentieth century the hope of this verse drove what is called the ecumenical movement, the effort to bring separated churches closer. Many trace its start to a world missionary conference in Edinburgh in 1910. The World Council of Churches was founded at Amsterdam in 1948.
passages.ot:
The prophets longed for a divided people to be made one. Israel had split into two kingdoms, and Ezekiel heard God promise, “they will no longer be two nations and will never again be divided into two kingdoms” (Ezekiel 37:22). A psalm sings, “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony” (Psalm 133:1).

And the oneness of God's people was always meant to reach outward. God said to his servant, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Jesus prays for a oneness the world can see.
passages.hard:
Doesn't the divided church show that this prayer failed? The objection is old and strong. In the second century the critic Celsus mocked Christians for splitting into rival groups, and the scholar Origen recorded his charge in his reply, Against Celsus (book 3). Since then the churches of East and West have parted, the Western church split again in the 1500s, and Christians have fought wars against one another. Today there are many denominations. If Jesus prayed for unity so that the world would believe, the skeptic says, then Christians' quarrels are the best argument against them.

It is better to admit this plainly. Christians are divided, and the division has done real harm. Every tradition has had a hand in it, and none can point only at the others.

Christians answer in different ways. Origen replied that serious things like medicine and philosophy also have rival schools, and no one gives up medicine because doctors disagree. Many Christians say the prayer is being answered whenever believers of different nations and churches know one another as brothers and sisters in Christ, sharing one Lord, “one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5). Others say the visible divisions are a wound that must not be made comfortable, and that the prayer calls the churches to keep seeking a unity they do not yet have. These notes take no side among the churches. They only say that the prayer still stands over every one of them.
passages.asks:
You were in Jesus' mind the night before he died: ‘those who will believe in Me through their message’. Ask what it means that he prayed for you by name, as it were, before you were born.

Then ask about the Christians you find hardest to call brothers and sisters, the ones who worship, vote or believe differently from you on lesser things. The world, Jesus said, will look at how his people love one another. Unity may start a long way from councils and covenants. It may start with the person you have written off.
